question: to the Commission Friedrich Pürner (NI) Subject:

The Commission’s proposal for the next multiannual financial framework includes the establishment of a European Competitiveness Fund to invest in strategic technologies across the internal market. Union-wide digital solutions, interoperable portals and an enhanced exchange of health data are envisaged, alongside the integration of the EU4Health programme into this fund. Independent investigations1 point to the risks associated with expanding the role of private tech companies in health policy, for instance by granting them access to publicly financed medical data sets for the purpose of developing AI-powered decision-support systems that can then be sold back to the public sector. The COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that caution must be exercised. The broad integration of health data raises issues of corporate oversight in addition to concerns relating to data protection, confidentiality and informed consent, as well as patient safety. Algorithmic tools can help to standardise diagnoses and treatments, but they can also be misleading, while large-scale systems tend to be less reliable, more unstable and susceptible to structural dependencies. 1.
Which technologies are to be prioritised and what are the risks associated with a potential dependence on big tech companies – including the scaling of other health services and medical care?
How is the Commission ensuring compliance with Article 168(7) TFEU, and how does it guarantee democratic accountability while preventing the commodification of health?
European Research Council (ERC), ID: 804985.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The European Competitiveness Fund does not favour any specific technology or provider. In line with the Apply AI Strategy1, the Commission supports the uptake of trustworthy AI, fostering innovation while mitigating risks and strengthening Europe’s technological sovereignty. This aligns with the Data Union Strategy2, which aims to scale up access to highquality data for AI and innovation, and safeguard the EU data sovereignty to strengthen the global position on international data flows. In the field of health, the Commission promotes secure and interoperable access to health data, notably through the European Health Data Space (EHDS) Regulation3. The EHDS establishes a common framework for the exchange and use of electronic health data across the EU. It strengthens individuals’ access to and control over their personal electronic health data while enabling the reuse of certain data for public interest purposes, policy-making and scientific research, subject to strict conditions and safeguards. Regarding Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU4, the Commission fully respects Member States’ competences for the organisation and delivery of health services. EU action focuses on supporting cooperation and facilitating cross-border data exchange, including through MyHealth@EU5. Democratic accountability is ensured through EU legislation adopted by the co-legislators and through established oversight mechanisms. Both the EHDS Regulation and General Data Protection Regulation6 provide strict safeguards governing access to and use of health data, helping prevent misuse or inappropriate commercial exploitation.
